newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end higher, weather boosts new crop.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end higher, weather boosts new crop.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures posted double-digit gains on Tuesday in reaction to forecasts for hot, dry weather which could stress crops during the blooming phase, traders said.
"New crop is a function of weather," Bill Biedermann, director of research for Allendale Inc, said. "We're going to go up every day until it rains, then we're going limit down."

Forecasts called for a cool week, followed by warmer temperatures this weekend with no significant chance for rain in Illinois until August 6. USDA's weekly crop update showed no improvement in soybean ratings despite last week's rains.

August also closed higher but reports of heavy farmer selling limited advances. Soybean crushers said purchases of old crop soybeans were brisk in Illinois and Indiana early Tuesday and some basis bids were falling in response.

"The old crop and the new crop started to decouple a little bit because the cash market is crashing on heavy farm movement," Biedermann said. "The demand for the old crop beans has gone downhill. Farmers seem to be letting go."
Soybeans ended 17-1/2 to 9-1/4 cents per bushel higher with new crop November up 17-1/4 cents at $6.36-1/2 a bushel and August up 9-1/4 at $7.67.
Cash soybean basis levels were down sharply.

Biedermann said end-users were reluctant to carry inventories of old crop soybeans with prospects of a bumper new crop in the fields. He noted cash prices in Illinois for August soybeans were at $1.39 a bushel over the November. New crop supplies were quoted at 45 cents under the November.
November soybeans traded as high as $6.41 per bushel, the highest since June 30 when USDA surprised the market by estimating 1997 U.S. soybean plantings at 70.9 million acres.
That acreage report sent soybean futures tumbling the 30-cent-per-bushel daily limit and set a bearish tone that the market was unable to shake for several weeks.
On the day, Refco Inc bought four million bushels Nov, Lind-Waldock and FIMAT Futures each bought three million Nov and Cargill Inc bought two million Nov, traders said.

Goldenberg-Hehmeyer spread one million November/August at $1.31 to $1.32, premium August, Continental Grain spread one million November/September at 41 cents, premium September, and Smith Barney spread one million August/November at $1.30, premium August, traders said.
In options, Lind-Waldock bought 500 November $6.50 calls at 27 cents and sold 500 November $6.00 puts at 13 cents. Cargill Investor Services bought 200 November $6.00 puts at 14 cents.
Volatility in the November was pegged at 25 percent.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 56,000 contracts, against Monday's actual volume of 46,907 contracts. Options volume was pegged at 16,000, against Monday's 14,168.
